title: Love and Hisses and sideline musicians in films
summary: His acting in Love and Hisses was only waving a baton while a record played; union rules required real musicians on camera, and Los Angeles had separate Black and white locals.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: "Love and Kisses," 19 -- "Love and Hisses," excuse me. That's the one you mentioned. 1937, 84 minutes, directed by Sidney Lanfield. Second round in a
screen feud started in, "Wake Up and Live," between Walter Winchell and Ben Bernie, with Simone Simone supplying the romance. Charlie Barnet has a small acting part.
Which consisted of standing in front of a band and waving a baton and trying to look like the band was really playing.
No, they were playing a record back. It had been recorded. Everybody that was in the picture was -- not one of them was on the record. Sideline, they call that.
They have to. The musicians' union requires that.
But the musicians' union, apparently, never took any action or gave a damn about things like the black musicians not being able to be photographed in the film, right?
No, they got paid, see? So there wasn't any -- wasn't anything they could do about it.
Do you think the union might even be happier because more musicians got paid because they had to have extra musicians to come in and sit on camera?
That's quite possible. Of course don't forget, in those days, I mean there were two locals in Los
Angeles. There was a black local and a white local.
